passages.p4:
For much of the last century, wetlands were treated as wasteland: marshes were drained for farms and lakes were filled for housing. Only later did planners notice what had been lost. A wetland stores water during heavy rain and releases it slowly, reducing floods downstream; it filters sediment and some pollutants; it recharges groundwater; and it supports fish, birds and the livelihoods built on them.

When a city builds over its lakes, the rain that once collected there must go somewhere, and it often goes into streets and homes. Restoring a wetland is possible but slow, and the original web of life rarely returns in full. Protecting the wetlands that still exist is far cheaper than rebuilding them, yet protection is often weak, because the benefits are spread across many people while the profit from building is concentrated in a few hands.
passages.p5:
Small loans to poor women were once hailed as a near-certain route out of poverty. The early evidence was striking: borrowers started businesses, repaid at high rates and often gained a stronger voice in their households. Later, more careful studies painted a quieter picture. On average, access to credit helped households cope with bad times and allowed some to invest, but it did not lift most of them out of poverty. Where too many lenders competed for the same borrowers, some households took one loan to repay another and slid into debt.

None of this means small loans are useless. It means they are a tool with limits — most useful alongside savings services, insurance and access to markets, and harmful when pushed without regard to whether borrowers can repay.
passages.p6: Public trust in science does not depend only on whether scientists are right. It depends also on whether people believe scientists are honest about what they do not know. During fast-moving crises, advice must often change as evidence builds up. When officials present early guidance as settled fact and later reverse it, many people conclude that they were misled, even if the change was a sign of science working properly. Explaining uncertainty openly — saying what is known, what is suspected and what would change the advice — can feel weak at the time, but it protects credibility over the long run.
passages.t2:
A family's monthly budget of ₹60,000 is divided as follows:
Item | Share of budget
Rent | 25%
Food | 30%
Transport | 10%
Education | 15%
Savings | 20%

questions.q: Which one of the following best reflects the main idea of the passage?
o: Urban floods are caused mainly by heavy rainfall.
Restored wetlands are as valuable as natural ones.
Wetlands provide several services, and the cost of losing them is easy to overlook.
Cities should stop building new houses.
questions.e: The passage lists what wetlands do — flood control, filtering, recharge, livelihoods — and shows how their loss was noticed only later and is costly to undo.

questions.q: According to the passage, why is the protection of wetlands often weak?
o: Restoring wetlands is cheaper than protecting them.
Laws forbid the protection of wetlands in cities.
The benefits are spread over many people, while the profit from building goes to a few.
questions.e: The last sentence gives this reason directly.

questions.q:
With reference to the passage, which of the following can be inferred?
1. Filling lakes can make urban flooding worse.
2. Restoration fully recreates the original wetland ecosystem.
questions.e: Rain that once collected in lakes 'often goes into streets and homes' (1). The passage says the original web of life 'rarely returns in full', so 2 is wrong.

questions.q: The author's view of small loans to the poor is best described as
o: balanced, recognising both benefits and limits
questions.e: The author reports real benefits, then the more modest findings and risks, and concludes that small loans are 'a tool with limits'.

questions.q: Which one of the following is mentioned in the passage as a risk of small loans?
o: Households taking one loan to repay another
Banks refusing to lend to the poor
Women losing their voice in the household
questions.e: Where lenders crowded in, some households borrowed to repay earlier loans and fell into debt.

questions.q:
With reference to the passage, the following assumptions have been made:
1. Findings from early studies may change when examined more carefully.
2. Credit by itself is enough to end poverty.
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
questions.e: The contrast between striking early evidence and 'more careful studies' assumes early findings can be revised (1). The passage says credit did not lift most households out of poverty, contradicting 2.

questions.q: Which one of the following best reflects the crux of the passage?
o: Scientists should avoid giving advice during a crisis.
Being open about uncertainty helps keep public trust when advice has to change.
The public cannot understand scientific uncertainty.
Changes in advice show that science is unreliable.
questions.e: The passage says presenting early advice as fact damages trust when it is reversed, while explaining uncertainty protects credibility.

questions.q: As used in the passage, the word 'credibility' most nearly means
questions.e: Credibility here is whether people believe what scientists and officials say.

questions.q: A can finish a piece of work in 10 days and B in 15 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves. In how many more days will B finish the remaining work?
questions.e: Together they do 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 a day; in 4 days, 2/3. B finishes the remaining 1/3 at 1/15 a day in 5 days.

questions.q: 40 litres of a mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 2?
questions.e: Milk 30 L, water 10 L. For 3 : 2, water must be 20 L, so add 10 L.

questions.q: The HCF and LCM of two numbers are 12 and 360 respectively. If one number is 72, what is the other?
questions.e: Product of the numbers = HCF × LCM = 4320. Other number = 4320 ÷ 72 = 60. (Check: HCF(72, 60) = 12, LCM = 360.)

questions.q: The price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percentage must a household reduce its consumption so that its expenditure on sugar stays the same?
questions.e: New price is 5/4 of the old, so consumption must be 4/5 of the old — a cut of 1/5 = 20%.

questions.q: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 7:20?
What is the sum of the first 20 odd natural numbers?
questions.e: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², so 20² = 400.

questions.q: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 8?
A car covers the first half of a journey at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
questions.e: For equal distances, average speed = 2 × 40 × 60/(40 + 60) = 48 km/h.

questions.q: How many three-digit numbers can be formed in which every digit is even (digits may repeat)?
questions.e: Even digits: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. The first digit cannot be 0 (4 choices); the other two have 5 each: 4 × 5 × 5 = 100.

questions.q: What comes next in the series 3, 8, 18, 38, 78, ?
questions.e: Each term is twice the previous one plus 2: 78 × 2 + 2 = 158.

questions.q: What comes next in the letter series B, E, I, N, ?
questions.e: The gaps grow by one: +3, +4, +5, +6. N (14) + 6 = T (20).

questions.q: In a class of 45 students, Asha ranks 12th from the top. What is her rank from the bottom?
questions.e: Rank from bottom = 45 − 12 + 1 = 34.

questions.q:
Statement: The government has made helmets compulsory for pillion riders on two-wheelers.
Assumptions:
I. Pillion riders face a risk of head injury in accidents.
II. Most pillion riders already wear helmets.
Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
o: Both Assumption I and Assumption II
Neither Assumption I nor Assumption II
questions.e: A rule requiring helmets assumes there is a head-injury risk (I). If most already wore helmets, the rule would be less needed, so II is not assumed.

questions.q: Four boxes A, B, C and D have different weights. A is heavier than B but lighter than C. D is heavier than C. Which box is the second heaviest?
questions.e: The order is D > C > A > B, so C is second heaviest.

questions.q: Which one of the following numbers is the odd one out?
questions.e: 169, 225 and 289 are perfect squares (13², 15², 17²); 343 = 7³ is a cube, not a square.

questions.q: How much does the family spend on food and education together each month?
If the rent rises by 20% and the family keeps its total budget the same by cutting only its savings, what share of the budget will savings now be?
questions.e: Rent ₹15,000 rises by ₹3,000. Savings fall from ₹12,000 to ₹9,000, which is 15% of ₹60,000.
